title: Amortization of R&E
description: Section 174 amortization required spreading research expenditures over 5 years (domestic) or 15 (foreign); Section 174A restored domestic expensing.
summary: Section 174 amortization is the U.S. tax rule requiring businesses to capitalize research and experimental (R&E) expenditures, including software development, and recover them over 5 years (domestic, 2022–2024) or 15 years (foreign). Public Law 119-21 added Section 174A, restoring immediate domestic R&E deductions for tax years beginning after 2024, while foreign R&E stays on 15-year amortization.

body.text: Section 174 amortization is the U.S. tax rule requiring businesses to capitalize research and experimental (R&E) expenditures, including software development, and recover them over 5 years (domestic, 2022–2024) or 15 years (foreign). Public Law 119-21 added Section 174A, restoring immediate domestic R&E deductions for tax years beginning after 2024, while foreign R&E stays on 15-year amortization.

The federal income tax treatment of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures in the United States under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 underwent a structural transformation beginning in tax year 2022, followed by a major statutory bifurcation enacted in July 2025. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Public Law 115-97, § 13206), Congress eliminated the longstanding statutory option allowing businesses to immediately deduct R&E costs in the taxable year paid or incurred, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. For taxable years beginning in 2022, 2023, and 2024, TCJA-amended IRC Section 174 mandated that all "specified research or experimental" (SRE) expenditures—explicitly expanded by statute to encompass all computer software development costs—be charged to a capital account and amortized ratably over 5 years (60 months) for domestic research conducted within the United States, or 15 years (180 months) for foreign research conducted outside the United States, starting at the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures were paid or incurred. Because the mandatory midpoint (half-year) convention limits first-year recovery of 5-year domestic R&E to 10% of total expenditure and 15-year foreign R&E to 3.33% of total expenditure, a corporate taxpayer incurring $1,000,000 in domestic R&E under the TCJA regime experienced an immediate first-year taxable income increase of $900,000 and an unavoidable cash-tax increase of $189,000 at the 21% statutory corporate tax rate under IRC Section 11(b).

Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21 added IRC Section 174A, which restores immediate current deductions—or an optional election under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize over a period of at least 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits—for domestic R&E expenditures, including domestic software development, paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Concurrently, Section 70302(b)(1) of Public Law 119-21 amended IRC Section 174 so that for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, mandatory capitalization and 15-year midpoint amortization under Section 174 apply exclusively to foreign R&E expenditures. Furthermore, Section 70302(f) of Public Law 119-21 and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 authorize taxpayers to elect to recover remaining unamortized TCJA domestic SRE capital account balances from 2022 through 2024 either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a 2-taxable-year period, and permit eligible small business taxpayers to elect retroactive application of Section 174A back to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021.

Second, regarding the legislative disposition of H.R. 7024 in the 118th Congress, earlier compliance commentary frequently referred to H.R. 7024 (the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024) as pending legislation. In the official congressional record, after passing the U.S. House of Representatives on January 31, 2024, by a bipartisan vote of 357–70, H.R. 7024 failed to achieve cloture in the U.S. Senate on August 1, 2024, by a vote of 48–44 on Roll Call Vote No. 230, and expired upon the sine die adjournment of the 118th Congress prior to the enactment of Public Law 119-21 in the 119th Congress.

Third, regarding the procedural mechanics of Form 3115 versus the simplified statement in lieu and modified Section 481(a) adjustments, general compliance summaries often state that adopting TCJA-amended Section 174 requires filing Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) on a cut-off basis. Under IRS Revenue Procedure 2023-11 and Revenue Procedure 2024-9, the requirement to file Form 3115 was specifically waived for the taxpayer's first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, in favor of a simplified written statement in lieu of Form 3115 applied on a cut-off basis with no IRC Section 481(a) adjustment. Conversely, if a taxpayer changes its accounting method to comply with TCJA Section 174 in a subsequent taxable year—after the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021—filing Form 3115 is mandatory and the change is not executed on a cut-off basis; instead, the taxpayer must calculate a modified Section 481(a) adjustment accounting strictly for SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021.

Fourth, regarding the partial obsoletion of Revenue Procedure 2000-50, broad assertions that Revenue Procedure 2000-50 is entirely obsolete for amounts paid or incurred after 2021 require technical precision. As clarified by Section 5 of IRS Notice 2024-12 and Section 3 of Revenue Procedure 2024-9, only Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (governing the costs of developing computer software) is obsoleted, and strictly for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Section 5 continues to apply to taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021, and the remaining provisions of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (governing acquired, leased, or licensed computer software) remain in full legal force.

Fifth, regarding contract research "excluded SRE product rights" and selective reliance under Notice 2024-12, while Section 6 of Notice 2023-63 established the foundational "risks and rights" contract research framework, Section 3 of Notice 2024-12 modified that test to establish a crucial safe harbor for "excluded SRE product rights". This modification confirms that a research provider bearing no financial risk does not incur capitalizable SRE expenditures merely because it acquires an SRE product right that is separately bargained for or restricted solely to performing contract research for the recipient. Furthermore, Section 4 of Notice 2024-12 eliminated the original "all-or-nothing" reliance rule in Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63, permitting taxpayers to rely selectively on individual sections of Notice 2023-63 provided they are applied consistently.
Executive Overview: The Paradigm Shift and Statutory Evolution of R&E Tax Recovery

From its original codification in the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 through taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021, former IRC Section 174 resolved administrative disputes over the indeterminate useful life of research expenditures by offering businesses three flexible cost recovery mechanisms. First, taxpayers could deduct R&E expenditures currently as an expense in the taxable year paid or incurred under former Section 174(a). Second, taxpayers could elect to capitalize and amortize those expenditures ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realized benefits from the expenditures under former Section 174(b). Third, taxpayers could charge the expenditures to a capital account—or alternatively make an annual election under IRC Section 59(e)(2)(B) to amortize qualified expenditures ratably over a 10-year period to mitigate alternative minimum tax adjustments or preserve net operating loss carryforwards. By permitting 100% immediate expensing in Year 1, the pre-TCJA statutory architecture aligned income tax deductions directly with current-year cash outlays, eliminating working capital friction for research-intensive enterprises.

Under Section 13206(a) and (e) of the TCJA (Public Law 115-97, enacted December 22, 2017, 131 Stat. 2054, 2111), Congress enacted a delayed revenue-raising offset that eliminated immediate expensing for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under TCJA-amended Section 174(a), taxpayers were required to charge all specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures to a capital account and recover them ratably over a 5-year (60-month) period for domestic research or a 15-year (180-month) period for foreign research (within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)), commencing at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures were paid or incurred. This mandatory deferral severely compressed corporate operating cash flow, artificially inflated current-year taxable income relative to economic profit, and forced a structural overhaul of enterprise cost accounting and quarterly tax provision workflows.

The statutory landscape shifted fundamentally once again on July 4, 2025, when Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, 191, the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act or OBBBA). Rather than repealing R&E amortization across all jurisdictions, Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 bifurcated the federal R&E tax regime into two parallel statutory sections effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. For domestic R&E expenditures, Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21 added IRC Section 174A(a), which restores immediate current deductibility by providing that, notwithstanding IRC Section 263, there shall be allowed as a deduction any domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business. Alternatively, under Section 174A(c), taxpayers may elect on a timely filed return (including extensions) to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures.

Conversely, for foreign R&E expenditures, Section 70302(b)(1) of Public Law 119-21 amended IRC Section 174 so that its title and operative provisions apply exclusively to "foreign research or experimental expenditures". Under amended Section 174(b), foreign research or experimental expenditures are defined as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that are attributable to foreign research within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)—namely, any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. Under amended Section 174(a)(1) and (2), no immediate deduction is permitted for foreign R&E; taxpayers must continue to charge all foreign R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a 15-year (180-month) period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which paid or incurred.

body.text: The structural interaction between R&E cost recovery under IRC Sections 174 and 174A and the Research and Development Tax Credit under IRC Section 41 represents a paramount compliance and modeling challenge for corporate tax departments. The pool of expenditures governed by Section 174 and post-2024 Section 174A is substantially broader than the restrictive subset of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) eligible for the Section 41 tax credit. Moreover, from an economic perspective, whenever R&E expenditures are required or elected to be amortized over 5 or 15 years rather than deducted immediately, the time value of money erodes the Net Present Value (NPV) of the tax deduction. At corporate discount rates, this deferral substantially diminished the net economic incentive provided by the Section 41 credit for domestic research during the 2022–2024 TCJA window and imposes a permanent capital-cost penalty on foreign research conducted outside the United States.
Regulatory Foundations: Mechanics of IRC Section 174 and Section 174A Capitalization
Delineation of Research or Experimental and Software Development Expenditures

To execute accurate tax compliance under IRC Sections 174 and 174A, corporate tax auditors must distinguish research or experimental expenditures from ordinary and necessary business expenses deductible under IRC Section 162. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) and Section 4.02 of IRS Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919), R&E expenditures encompass two foundational categories of costs paid or incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business.

First, under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2, experimental or laboratory R&D costs encompass activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(3), a "product" is defined broadly to include any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property to be used by the taxpayer in its trade or business or held for sale, lease, or license. Uncertainty exists for Section 174 purposes if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product. Under Section 4.03 of Notice 2023-63, allocable SRE costs include direct and indirect labor—specifically wages, stock-based compensation, payroll taxes, vacation and sick pay, and employee benefits (explicitly excluding severance pay) for employees and contractors directly performing, supervising, or directly supporting research—along with materials and supplies, depreciation or depletion allowances on property used in research, allocable overhead (such as facility rent, utilities, and security allocable to research facilities), and patent procurement costs.

Second, under IRC Section 174(c)(3) (for foreign R&E and 2022–2024 domestic R&E) and IRC Section 174A(d)(3) (for post-2024 domestic R&E), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any computer software is statutorily mandated to be treated as a research or experimental expenditure. As Section 4.02(2) of Notice 2023-63 confirms, software development expenditures are statutorily classified as R&E expenditures by operation of law, regardless of whether the underlying software development activities satisfy the technical uncertainty standard of Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2. Consequently, routine application coding that faces no technological uncertainty is nonetheless swept into the statutory R&E regime.

Both Section 174(c)(1)–(2) and Section 174A(d)(1)–(2) exclude two statutory categories from direct R&E treatment: (1) expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land, or of property to be used in connection with research that is subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC Section 167 or depletion under IRC Section 611 (although the annual depreciation and depletion allowances themselves on such research equipment or facilities are treated as R&E expenditures); and (2) exploration expenditures paid or incurred for the purpose of ascertaining the existence, location, extent, or quality of any deposit of ore or other mineral, including oil and gas. Additionally, Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(6) excludes ordinary quality control testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising or promotions, the costs of acquiring another person's patent, model, production, or process, and research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects.

A critical regulatory clarification governs the status of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (2000-2 C.B. 601). Prior to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 permitted taxpayers to treat the costs of developing computer software in a manner similar to Section 174 by either deducting them currently or capitalizing and amortizing them ratably over 60 months from the completion of development or 36 months from the date the software was placed in service pursuant to IRC Section 167(f)(1). Generalized statements that Revenue Procedure 2000-50 is entirely obsolete for amounts paid or incurred after 2021 require two precise legal qualifications established in Section 5 of IRS Notice 2024-12 (2024-5 I.R.B. 616) and Section 3 of Revenue Procedure 2024-9 (2024-5 I.R.B. 628). First, only Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (which governed the costs of developing computer software) is removed as obsolete; the remaining sections of Revenue Procedure 2000-50—specifically the administrative safe harbors governing acquired, leased, or licensed computer software—remain valid and unaffected by Section 174. Second, the obsoletion of Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 applies strictly to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. For fiscal-year taxpayers who paid or incurred software development costs during calendar year 2022 within a fiscal taxable year that began on or before December 31, 2021, Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 continued to govern. Furthermore, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 remains obsolete because software development is statutorily governed by IRC Section 174A(d)(3) (domestic) and IRC Section 174(c)(3) (foreign), domestic software development costs once again qualify for a 100% immediate deduction under Section 174A(a) or elective amortization over at least 60 months under Section 174A(c).
Geographical Amortization Disparity, Midpoint Convention, and Property Dispositions

The geographical location where research activities are physically performed dictates the statutory recovery schedule, creating a profound tax wedge for multinational enterprises. As illustrated in Example 6.05 of IRS Notice 2023-63, the applicable amortization period depends strictly on the physical location where the research activities are performed—whether conducted in-house by employees or externally by a third-party contractor—and not on the tax residence, place of incorporation, or domicile of the taxpayer paying for the research or holding the resulting intellectual property.

During the TCJA mandatory capitalization period (taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025), domestic SRE expenditures were amortized over 5 years (60 months), whereas foreign SRE expenditures were amortized over 15 years (180 months). Following the enactment of Public Law 119-21 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, this geographical disparity has widened dramatically: domestic R&E is 100% deductible in Year 1 under Section 174A(a), whereas foreign R&E remains locked into a mandatory 15-year (180-month) amortization schedule under Section 174(a)(2)(B). From a strategic standpoint, this permanent statutory asymmetry alters global transfer pricing and R&D supply chain economics, heavily penalizing U.S. corporations that outsource software engineering or contract research to offshore subsidiaries or foreign third-party vendors while incentivizing the onshoring of laboratory facilities and technical personnel within the United States.

Under IRC Section 174(a)(2)(B), mandatory amortization begins with the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures are paid or incurred. For a standard 12-month taxable year, this mandatory half-year convention dictates that only 6 months of amortization may be claimed in Year 1, regardless of whether the expenditures were incurred in January or December. Compounding the economic cost of delayed amortization, IRC Section 174(d) enforces a rigid lock-in rule upon the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property. If any property with respect to which Section 174 expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 5- or 15-year amortization period, no accelerated loss deduction under IRC Section 165 is allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the taxpayer must continue amortizing the unrecovered expenditures over the remainder of the statutory amortization period. Crucially, under Section 70302(b)(1)(C) of Public Law 119-21, effective for dispositions, retirements, or abandonments of foreign R&E property occurring after May 12, 2025, Congress further tightened Section 174(d) to specify that no deduction or reduction to amount realized is permitted upon disposition. This statutory amendment closes a transaction-planning avenue in which taxpayers previously argued that unamortized Section 174 basis could offset taxable capital gain as adjusted basis under IRC Section 1001 upon the taxable sale of an R&D project or subsidiary asset.
Procedural Compliance Mechanism: Accounting Method Changes and Legislative History
Accounting Method Change Rules: Cut-Off Basis, Statement in Lieu, and Form 3115

Under Section 13206(b) of the TCJA—and similarly under Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 for post-2024 transitions—transitioning to the statutory R&E accounting rules is treated as a change in method of accounting under IRC Sections 446(e) and 481 that is initiated by the taxpayer and executed with the automatic consent of the Secretary of the Treasury.

A rigorous examination of authoritative IRS procedural guidance—specifically Revenue Procedure 2023-11 (2023-3 I.R.B. 417, which modified and superseded Revenue Procedure 2023-8), Revenue Procedure 2023-24 (2023-28 I.R.B. 1207), Revenue Procedure 2024-9 (2024-5 I.R.B. 628), Revenue Procedure 2024-34, Revenue Procedure 2025-8, and Revenue Procedure 2025-28—reveals a strict procedural dichotomy that depends on the specific taxable year in which the accounting method change is implemented.

When a taxpayer adopted TCJA-amended Section 174 in its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, under Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change No. 265, the change was required to be implemented strictly on a cut-off basis. Under a cut-off basis, R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021, remain governed by the taxpayer's prior method of accounting, and no IRC Section 481(a) catch-up adjustment is either required or permitted. However, contrary to simplified assertions that Form 3115 was universally required for initial adoption, the IRS waived the requirement to file Form 3115 for that first effective taxable year and instead authorized taxpayers to attach a concise written statement in lieu of Form 3115 to their original federal income tax return (without filing a duplicate copy with the IRS in Ogden, Utah). Additionally, under a special administrative transition rule in Revenue Procedure 2023-11, taxpayers who filed a federal return on or before January 17, 2023, for a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, were deemed to have complied with the Section 446 method change procedures if they properly capitalized and amortized SRE expenditures and reported them on Part VI of Form 4562 (Depreciation and Amortization).

Conversely, if a taxpayer failed to adopt TCJA Section 174 in its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, or subsequently changed its method of accounting in a later taxable year (such as 2023 or 2024, including changes made to conform to the substantive rules of Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12), the simplified statement in lieu of Form 3115 cannot be used. Instead, the taxpayer is required to complete and file a formal Form 3115 (with an attachment detailing the types of SRE expenditures, the taxable years incurred, and a required declaration), and the change is not executed on a cut-off basis. Rather, the taxpayer must compute a modified Section 481(a) adjustment that takes into account exclusively SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Furthermore, taxpayers making a late compliance change in the taxable year immediately subsequent to the first effective year forfeit audit protection for SRE expenditures paid or incurred in that first taxable year.

For post-2024 transitions under Public Law 119-21 (OBBBA) and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (which modified Section 7.02 of Revenue Procedure 2025-23 under Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change No. 273), adopting the new Section 174A(a) immediate deduction method or the Section 174A(c) elective amortization method for domestic R&E paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, is likewise treated as a taxpayer-initiated automatic accounting method change applied on a cut-off basis with no Section 481(a) adjustment. In addition, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 operationalizes two pivotal transition elections enacted under Section 70302(f) of Public Law 119-21. First, under Section 70302(f)(2), all taxpayers holding remaining unamortized domestic SRE capital account balances attributable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to deduct those unamortized balances either 100% in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a 2-taxable-year period beginning with that first taxable year. Second, under Section 70302(f)(1), eligible small business taxpayers—defined as taxpayers meeting the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test and not classified as tax shelters—may elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to domestic R&E paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, by filing amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) for partnerships. Because Public Law 119-21 did not extend the general IRC Section 6511 statute of limitations on credit or refund claims, retroactive elections for the 2022 taxable year were required to be filed on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026, or 3 years from the filing date of the original 2022 tax return.

body.text: Legislative Trajectory: Expiration of H.R. 7024 and Enactment of Public Law 119-21

During 2023 and 2024, tax compliance literature cautioned corporate tax departments against delaying Section 174 implementation in anticipation of retroactive legislative relief such as H.R. 7024. While the compliance directive to follow enacted law rather than pending bills was sound, the historical legislative trajectory requires exact documentation. Specifically, Title II, Section 201 of H.R. 7024 (the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024, reported in House Report 118-353 on January 23, 2024) proposed enacting a temporary IRC Section 174A to suspend mandatory domestic R&E capitalization retroactively for taxable years 2022 through 2025. Although the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 7024 by an overwhelming bipartisan margin of 357–70 on January 31, 2024, the legislation stalled in the U.S. Senate. On August 1, 2024, the Senate voted 48–44 on Roll Call Vote No. 230 on a motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 7024—falling 12 votes short of the required 60-vote supermajority—and the bill expired with the close of the 118th Congress. Subsequently, in the 119th Congress, lawmakers enacted Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025, permanently codifying IRC Section 174A for domestic R&E paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (with retroactive relief restricted to eligible small businesses and accelerated 1- or 2-year recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 balances for larger taxpayers), while leaving mandatory 15-year capitalization under IRC Section 174 permanently in place for foreign R&E.
Cross-Code Interplay: IRC Section 41 R&D Credit and Cascading Corporate Tax Impacts
Prerequisite Relationship and Cost Pool Divergence Between Sections 174/174A and Section 41

A frequent compliance error in corporate R&D accounting arises from conflating R&E expenditures governed by IRC Section 174 (or post-2024 Section 174A) with Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) eligible for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC Section 41. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), "qualified research" must satisfy a cumulative Four-Part Test, applied separately to each discrete business component—defined under Section 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer.

First, under the Section 174 / 174A Threshold Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), the research must be an activity with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified R&E expenditures under Section 174 (for taxable years 2022 through 2024) or as domestic R&E expenditures under Section 174A (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, as amended by Public Law 119-21). Second, under the Discovering Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—relying fundamentally on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—intended to eliminate uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. Third, under the Business Component or Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, explicitly excluding adaptations relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), substantially all—defined under Treasury Regulations as 80% or more, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that identifies the technical uncertainty, identifies one or more alternatives to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducts a systematic process of modeling, simulation, or trial-and-error evaluation of those alternatives.

Even when an activity satisfies all four components of Section 41(d), IRC Section 41(b) strictly restricts credit-eligible QREs to two narrow expenditure categories: (a) in-house research expenses—specifically employee W-2 wages as defined in IRC Section 3401(a) for qualified services (consisting of the direct conduct, direct supervision, or direct support of qualified research), tangible non-depreciable supplies used and consumed in the conduct of qualified research, and computer rental or cloud computing payments paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research; and (b) contract research expenses, generally limited to 65% of amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research (or 75% for payments to qualified research consortia and 100% for eligible energy research).

Consequently, the universe of Section 174 and Section 174A R&E expenditures is substantially broader than the subset of Section 41 QREs. Patent procurement costs—specifically patent attorneys' fees and government filing fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application—exemplify this statutory divergence: such costs are explicitly included as R&E expenditures under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1), yet are completely excluded from QREs under IRC Section 41 and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Research Tax Credit. Similarly, allocable overhead expenses (such as laboratory rent and utilities), depreciation allowances on research equipment, non-taxable employee fringe benefits excluded from IRC Section 3401(a) wages, routine software development lacking technological uncertainty, the remaining 35% of domestic third-party contract research payments, and 100% of foreign research expenses fall squarely within Section 174 or Section 174A but generate zero Section 41 tax credit.

Furthermore, taxpayers claiming the Section 41 credit must coordinate their R&E deduction or capital account with IRC Section 280C(c). Under Section 280C(c)(1) (as amended by Section 70302(b)(2)(B) of Public Law 119-21 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), a taxpayer must reduce its domestic R&E expenditures otherwise deductible or capitalizable under Section 174A by 100% of the amount of its Section 41(a) research credit—whereas during the 2022–2024 TCJA window, Section 280C(c)(1) reduced the capitalizable SRE account only to the extent the Section 41 credit exceeded the current-year amortization deduction—unless the taxpayer makes an irrevocable election on Item A of its original, timely filed Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) under Section 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced research credit (reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21%, yielding a net 79% credit).
Cascading Effects Across Sections 163(j), 250, 951A, and 263A
Mandatory capitalization and amortization of R&E expenditures trigger complex mathematical ripples across key domestic and international provisions of the Internal Revenue Code.

Under the Business Interest Expense Limitation of IRC Section 163(j), a taxpayer's deduction for business interest expense under Section 163(j)(1) is generally capped at the sum of business interest income, 30% of Adjusted Taxable Income (ATI), and floor plan financing interest. Because the computation of ATI under Section 163(j)(8) begins with tentative taxable income, deferring 90% of a domestic R&E deduction in Year 1 (under TCJA 5-year amortization) or 96.67% of a foreign R&E deduction (under 15-year amortization) inflates tentative taxable income and increases the 30% ATI interest deduction ceiling in the initial year of the amortization cycle. However, a crucial statutory nuance governs how ATI is defined: while general financial commentary often describes ATI as analogous to EBITDA, during the TCJA amortization window of 2022 through 2024, IRC Section 163(j)(8)(A)(v) required depreciation and amortization deductions to be subtracted when computing ATI—making ATI analogous to EBIT rather than EBITDA during those years and preventing Section 174 amortization deductions from being added back to ATI. Consequently, as prior years' capitalized R&E cohorts accumulate and generate larger annual amortization deductions—or when taxpayers deduct unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in 2025 and 2026 under Public Law 119-21—tentative taxable income is compressed, reversing the early-year expansion of the Section 163(j) interest limitation.

Within the international corporate tax regime governing Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII) under IRC Section 250 and Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) under IRC Section 951A, Section 4.04 of Notice 2023-63 mandates that R&E amortization deductions must be allocated and apportioned under Treasury Regulations §§ 1.861-8 and 1.861-17. A rigorous technical distinction governs the mechanics of FDII versus GILTI under these apportionment rules. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.250(b)-1(d)(3) and the IRS Instructions for Form 8993 (Section 250 Deduction for Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII) and Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI)), R&E deductions are treated as definitely related to "gross intangible income" within specific three-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code product categories and are apportioned using the sales method under Treasury Regulation § 1.861-17(d) (without applying the exclusive geographic apportionment rule of § 1.861-17(c)) to compute Deduction Eligible Income (DEI) and Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income (FDDEI). By deferring domestic R&E deductions during 2022–2024, mandatory capitalization artificially expanded DEI and FDDEI in Year 1 while depressing FDII deductions in subsequent years—and similarly, electing to deduct unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E balances in 2025 or 2026 under Public Law 119-21 significantly reduces FDDEI in those recovery years.

With respect to GILTI, however, Treasury Regulation § 1.861-17(b)(2) explicitly specifies that "gross intangible income" does not include dividends or inclusions under IRC Section 951A (GILTI). Thus, a U.S. corporation's own Section 174 or Section 174A R&E deductions are not apportioned directly against its GILTI inclusion under § 1.861-17. Instead, Section 174 impacts GILTI through two distinct structural channels: (1) at the Controlled Foreign Corporation (CFC) level, where a CFC's foreign R&E expenditures must be capitalized and amortized over 15 years under Section 174, immediately increasing the CFC's "tested income" under Section 951A(c)(2)(A) and inflating the U.S. shareholder's GILTI inclusion; and (2) at the U.S. shareholder level via the Section 250(a)(2) taxable income limitation (Form 8993, Lines 24–27), which caps the combined FDII and GILTI deduction (set at 37.5% for FDII and 50% for GILTI for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026, and scheduled to adjust to 33.34% and 40%, respectively, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026) at the domestic corporation's overall taxable income.

Finally, regarding Uniform Capitalization (UNICAP) and inventory accounting under IRC Section 263A, 26 U.S.C. § 263A(c)(2) (as amended by Public Law 119-21) provides that the UNICAP rules requiring capitalization of direct and indirect production costs into inventory or self-constructed assets explicitly do not apply to any amount allowable as a deduction under Section 174 or Section 174A. Furthermore, Section 4.04 of Notice 2023-63 states unequivocally that SRE expenditures may not be treated as ordinary and necessary expenses under Section 162 or capitalized into inventory or fixed assets under IRC Sections 195, 263(a), 263A, or 471. For manufacturing enterprises that historically embedded product engineering, prototype tooling, or R&D overhead into Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and ending inventory absorption pools under Section 263A, Section 7.02 of Revenue Procedure 2024-9 provides an automatic accounting method change to reclassify those SRE costs out of Section 263A inventory and into the mandatory Section 174 regime.

Corporate Estimated Tax Penalties and GAAP-to-Tax Financial Statement Divergence

The front-loaded spike in Year 1 taxable income directly impacts quarterly corporate estimated income tax obligations under IRC Section 6655. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6655(c)–(d), a calendar-year C corporation must remit four required quarterly installments (due April 15, June 15, September 15, and December 15), each equal to 25% of the "required annual payment"—defined as the lesser of 100% of the tax shown on the current-year return or 100% of the tax shown on the preceding 12-month year's return. However, under Section 6655(d)(2) and (g)(2), a "large corporation" (defined as any corporation, or predecessor corporation, that had taxable income of $1,000,000 or more during any of the 3 immediately preceding testing taxable years, excluding net operating loss and capital loss carrybacks or carryovers) is statutorily barred from relying on the prior-year tax safe harbor except for its first quarterly installment, and must recapture 100% of any first-installment reduction in its second quarterly installment due June 15. Consequently, if a corporation underestimates the taxable income add-back resulting from Section 174 capitalization—or fails to precisely model the annualized income installment safe harbor under Section 6655(e)—it incurs mandatory nondeductible underpayment penalties calculated at the IRC Section 6621 underpayment rate from each installment due date.

Furthermore, mandatory R&E capitalization creates a pronounced structural divergence between U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (U.S. GAAP) and federal income tax reporting. Under Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 730 (Research and Development)—which IRS examiners frequently review as a baseline audit step under Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.30.2—internal and company-sponsored research and development costs are charged to expense as incurred on the financial statement income statement. Because R&E expenditures are expensed immediately for book purposes under ASC 730 but capitalized and amortized over 5 or 15 years for tax purposes under IRC Section 174 (or electively under Section 174A(c)), the tax basis of the capitalized R&E asset exceeds its zero book basis. Under FASB ASC Topic 740 (Income Taxes), this deductible temporary difference generates a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) on the corporate balance sheet. For early-stage biotechnology, software, or hardware companies that incur net operating losses or cannot demonstrate under ASC 740 that it is "more likely than not" (a likelihood greater than 50%) that sufficient future taxable income will exist to realize the DTA, the company is required to record a valuation allowance offsetting the DTA. Recording a valuation allowance prevents the deferred tax benefit from offsetting the current tax provision, causing the current cash-tax spike from Section 174 capitalization to flow directly through to the income statement as a sharp increase in the company's GAAP effective tax rate. Additionally, businesses operating with cyclical, milestone-driven R&D outlays experience severe tax-basis income volatility, which can inadvertently trigger technical defaults under tax-adjusted cash flow or debt-service coverage covenants in commercial credit agreements.
Administrative Guidance Analysis: Software Development, Contract Research, and Cost Sharing under Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12

To resolve widespread compliance uncertainty following the TCJA amendments, the Department of the Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2023-63 (released September 8, 2023; published at 2023-39 I.R.B. 919) and subsequently clarified and modified that interim guidance in Notice 2024-12 (released December 22, 2023; published at 2024-5 I.R.B. 616).

A foundational procedural correction applies to how taxpayers rely on this administrative guidance. Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63 originally imposed a rigid "all-or-nothing" reliance rule, stipulating that any taxpayer choosing to rely on any individual rule in Sections 3 through 9 of Notice 2023-63 was required to rely on and apply all rules across Sections 3 through 9. Because this requirement would have forced taxpayers who had already filed 2022 tax returns to either amend returns or forfeit reliance on favorable provisions (such as the software or contract research exclusions), Section 4 of Notice 2024-12 modified Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63 to eliminate the requirement that taxpayers rely on all rules. Under Notice 2024-12, taxpayers may selectively rely on individual sections within Sections 3 through 9 of Notice 2023-63 (as modified by Notice 2024-12) for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, provided they apply the chosen rules consistently—with the sole statutory exception that taxpayers may not rely on Section 7 of Notice 2023-63 for SRE expenditures paid or incurred with respect to property contributed to, distributed from, or transferred from a partnership.
Activity-Based Delineation of Software Development Costs

Section 5 of Notice 2023-63 establishes a detailed activity-based framework to separate capitalizable software development under IRC Section 174(c)(3) (and post-2024 Section 174A(d)(3)) from routine, non-R&E information technology operations deductible under IRC Section 162 or depreciable under IRC Section 167(f).

Under Section 5.02(1) of Notice 2023-63, "computer software" is defined broadly to encompass any computer program or routine (and any sequence of code) designed to cause a computer to perform a desired function or set of functions, together with the documentation required to describe and maintain that program or routine. This definition encompasses system software, programming software, application software, embedded software, operating systems, executive systems, monitors, compilers, translators, assembly routines, utility programs, cloud-hosted Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms, internal-use enterprise software, and commercial software held for sale, lease, or license, while excluding databases unless the database is incidental to the operation of the software. Crucially, Section 5.02(2) defines "upgrades and enhancements" as modifications to existing computer software—explicitly including modifications to third-party purchased software—that result in additional functionality (enabling the software to perform tasks that it was previously incapable of performing) or that materially increase the speed or efficiency of the software.

Contract Research: The Risks and Rights Framework and Excluded SRE Product Rights Safe Harbor

In third-party and intercompany contract research arrangements, a central audit issue is determining whether the research recipient (the customer or payor funding the research), the research provider (the contractor or vendor performing the research), or both parties simultaneously must treat their respective costs as R&E expenditures.

Under Section 6.03 of Notice 2023-63, the tax treatment of costs paid or incurred by the research recipient continues to be governed by longstanding principles in Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(10) and (b)(3): payments made to a third party for research carried on in the recipient's behalf constitute R&E expenditures of the recipient if the research is performed upon the recipient's order and at the recipient's financial risk.

For the research provider, however, Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63 established a two-prong "risks and rights" test to determine whether the provider's costs of performing the contract are deductible ordinary cost of services under IRC Section 162 or capitalizable SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174 (or post-2024 Section 174A). Under Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63, a research provider must treat costs paid or incurred incident to performing contract research as SRE expenditures if either of the following two conditions is triggered.

First, under the Financial Risk Test, the provider's costs are SRE expenditures if, under the terms of the contract, the research provider bears financial risk—defined in Section 6.02(3) of Notice 2023-63 as the risk that the research provider may suffer a financial loss related to the failure of the research to produce the desired SRE product, as commonly occurs in fixed-price contracts or milestone-contingent fee structures where payment is conditioned on technical success.

Second, under the Exploitation or Use Rights Test ("SRE Product Right"), even if the research provider bears zero financial risk (such as in a pure cost-plus or time-and-materials service contract), the provider must still treat its performance costs as SRE expenditures if the provider has a right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit any resulting SRE product through sale, lease, or license—unless the provider can obtain that right only upon receiving explicit approval from another party to the arrangement that is unrelated to the provider within the meaning of IRC Section 267 or Section 707. Under Section 6.02(4) of Notice 2023-63, generic "know-how" gained by a research provider that is not subject to legal protection under domestic or foreign law does not constitute an SRE product.

Following the release of Notice 2023-63, tax practitioners identified that the literal wording of Section 6.04 threatened to cause punitive dual capitalization in routine commercial service arrangements where a contractor bears no financial risk (so the customer capitalizes the contract price under Section 6.03) but the contract grants the contractor a standard operational license to use the customer's background or foreground intellectual property solely to perform the contracted services for that customer, or where the contractor separately pays for a commercial license. To eliminate this unintended dual capitalization trap, Section 3 of Notice 2024-12 modified Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63 by introducing the "excluded SRE product right" safe harbor. Under this safe harbor, if a research provider does not bear financial risk under the contract and obtains only an excluded SRE product right (and no other SRE product right under the contract), the costs paid or incurred by the research provider to perform SRE activities on behalf of the research recipient are not SRE expenditures. An SRE product right qualifies as an excluded SRE product right if it satisfies either of two criteria: (1) the right is separately bargained for—meaning it arose from consideration other than the cost paid or incurred by the research provider to perform SRE activities under that contract; or (2) the right was acquired for the limited purpose of performing SRE activities under that contract or another contract with the research recipient.
Intercompany Cost Sharing Arrangements and CST Payments

Section 9 of Notice 2023-63 addresses the complex intersection between Section 174 capitalization and intercompany Cost Sharing Arrangements (CSAs) governed by the transfer pricing rules of Treasury Regulation § 1.482-7. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.482-7(a)(1) and (d), controlled participants in a qualified CSA agree to share Intangible Development Costs (IDCs) in proportion to their respective shares of Reasonably Anticipated Benefits (RAB) by making compensating Cost Sharing Transaction (CST) payments under Treasury Regulation § 1.482-7(j)(3)(i).

Prior to the TCJA amendments, when R&E was currently deductible, CST payments received by a controlled participant simply reduced that participant's current deductible IDCs, with any CST payment in excess of total IDCs treated as consideration for the use of land or tangible property. Because post-2021 IDCs incurred within a CSA pool may include both capitalizable SRE expenditures (such as foreign R&E under Section 174 or domestic R&E during the 2022–2024 TCJA window) and currently deductible non-SRE IDCs (or post-2024 domestic R&E expensed under Section 174A(a)), Section 9 of Notice 2023-63 modifies the mechanics of Treasury Regulation § 1.482-7(j)(3)(i). Specifically, CST payments received by a controlled participant must be allocated to proportionally reduce both the recipient participant's capitalizable SRE expenditures and its deductible non-SRE IDCs, with any CST payment exceeding the payor's ratable RAB share of total IDCs treated as taxable income to the recipient. Multinational groups operating CSAs between U.S. parent entities and foreign IP-holding subsidiaries must therefore maintain segregated sub-ledgers tracking domestic SRE, foreign SRE, and non-SRE IDC pools for every CSA participant.
Strategic Planning and Corporate Implementation Framework

To navigate the bifurcated compliance landscape of IRC Sections 174 and 174A, IRS Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12, and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, corporate tax departments should execute a structured four-pillar operational strategy.

First, enterprises should implement Three-Way General Ledger Cost Mapping and Jurisdictional Segregation. Tax departments should configure ERP and project-accounting architectures to classify all technical, engineering, laboratory, and IT expenditures at the point of original entry into three distinct tax buckets: (a) IRC §§ 174/174A R&E Expenditures, strictly sub-segmented by physical performance location between U.S.-performed domestic research eligible for immediate deduction under Section 174A(a) and non-U.S.-performed foreign research subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under Section 174(a)(2)(B); (b) IRC § 41 Credit-Eligible QREs, encompassing strictly domestic W-2 wages, tangible supplies, computer rental, and qualifying contract research meeting the four-part business-component test, tracked at the granular business-component level required for Section G of revised Form 6765 for taxable years beginning after 2025; and (c) Routine IRC § 162 Deductible Operating Expenses, capturing purchased software licenses, pre-coded parameter configuration, employee training, data migration execution, and post-deployment corrective debugging excluded under Sections 5.04 and 5.05 of Notice 2023-63.

Second, corporate tax teams must prioritize the Execution of Post-2024 OBBBA Method Changes and Unamortized TCJA Balance Recovery under Revenue Procedure 2025-28. Specifically, under Section 70302(f)(2) of Public Law 119-21 and Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change No. 273, taxpayers must model whether to deduct 100% of their remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE capital account balances in their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or amortize that unrecovered balance ratably over two taxable years (2025 and 2026). A single-year lump-sum deduction maximizes immediate cash-tax recovery, operating cash flow, and net present value, whereas electing a two-year ratable recovery may prove superior if a massive one-year deduction would otherwise trigger the IRC Section 250(a)(2) taxable income limitation—thereby permanently forfeiting 37.5% FDII and 50% GILTI deductions that cannot be carried forward—or compress Adjusted Taxable Income under IRC Section 163(j). Concurrently, eligible small business taxpayers satisfying the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts threshold should evaluate whether amending 2022–2024 returns under Section 70302(f)(1) before the applicable IRC Section 6511 statute of limitations expiration yields superior refund liquidity.

Third, multinational groups should integrate Net Present Value (NPV) Location Modeling into R&D site-selection and global workforce planning. Because Public Law 119-21 permanently restored 100% Year 1 expensing for domestic R&E under Section 174A(a) while retaining mandatory 15-year (180-month) midpoint amortization for foreign R&E under Section 174(a)(2)(B)—where only 3.33% is deductible in Year 1 and recovery stretches across 16 taxable years—the structural tax penalty on offshore R&D is wider than at any prior point in U.S. tax history. Corporate finance teams must incorporate both the 15-year foreign amortization NPV penalty (including its upward distortion of CFC tested income under IRC Section 951A) and the complete disallowance of foreign research under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F) when comparing the fully loaded after-tax cost of foreign versus domestic engineering centers.

Fourth, legal and tax departments should institute a mandatory Contractual Review Playbook for the "Risks and Rights" Test and Excluded SRE Product Rights. Prior to executing third-party vendor agreements or intercompany R&D service contracts, tax counsel must audit the intellectual property and payment clauses against Section 6 of Notice 2023-63 and Section 3 of Notice 2024-12. Where a corporate entity acts as a contract research provider and seeks to deduct its performance costs currently under IRC Section 162 (particularly crucial when the provider performs services outside the United States that would otherwise be trapped in 15-year foreign amortization under Section 174), contract language must explicitly establish that: (a) the provider bears no financial risk of loss upon technical failure (utilizing time-and-materials or non-contingent cost-plus pricing); and (b) any right granted to the provider to use resulting SRE products is either conditioned upon explicit prior approval by an unrelated party under IRC Sections 267 and 707 or drafted strictly within the boundaries of an "excluded SRE product right" under Section 3 of Notice 2024-12—meaning the license is restricted solely to performing SRE activities under contracts with that specific research recipient or is separately bargained and paid for via independent consideration.
